questions.q: As per the criteria table, drugs are best absorbed when their solubility is:
questions.exp: The absorption column of the criteria table requires lipid solubility, whereas the excretion column requires water solubility. (Book p5)

questions.q: For a drug to be excreted, the criteria table requires it to be:
questions.exp: Excretion needs water solubility and ionization - the water-soluble ionised form cannot be reabsorbed and is excreted. (Book p5)

questions.q: According to the criteria table, absorption of a drug requires it to be:
opts: Unionised with pH of medium equal to that of the drug
Ionised with pH of medium unequal to that of the drug
questions.exp: Absorption: lipid soluble, unionised, pH of medium equal to that of drug (relation of pH 'equal') and non-polar. (Book p5)

questions.q: In the criteria table, the 'relation of pH of medium' for EXCRETION is:
opts: Equal for acidic drugs and unequal for basic drugs
questions.exp: Excretion occurs when the pH of the drug and the pH of the medium are unequal, so the drug is ionised and trapped in urine. (Book p5)

questions.q: Which polarity favours absorption of a drug?
questions.exp: Non-polar drugs are absorbed; polar (ionised) drugs are excreted. (Book p5)

questions.q: The mnemonic LUNA stands for the criteria of:
opts: Absorption - Lipid, Unionised, pH relation equal, Non-polar
questions.exp: LUNA summarises absorption: Lipid, Unionised, Non-polar with pH of medium equal to that of the drug; its counterpart WIPE summarises excretion. (Book p5)

questions.q: The mnemonic WIPE stands for the criteria of:
opts: Excretion - Water soluble, Ionised, Polar, pH relation unequal
Absorption - Water soluble, Ionised, Polar, Absorption equal
Excretion - Water soluble, Ionised, Protein bound, Equal pH
Excretion - Water insoluble, Ionised, Polar, pH equal
questions.exp: WIPE denotes excretion: Water soluble, Ionised, Polar, with unequal pH of drug and medium. (Book p5)

questions.q: An acidic drug remains unionised in an acidic medium such as the:
questions.exp: Acidic drug in an acidic medium (stomach) stays unionised and lipid soluble, which is why aspirin is unionised in the stomach. (Book p5)

questions.q: A basic drug stays unionised in a basic medium such as the:
questions.exp: Basic drug in a basic medium (small intestine) remains unionised; the pair is stated as 'acidic drug - acidic medium: stomach; basic drug - basic medium: small intestine'. (Book p5)

questions.q: Aspirin, an acidic drug, is unionised in the stomach. This follows the rule that:
opts: An acidic drug stays unionised in an acidic medium
A basic drug stays unionised in an acidic medium
All drugs are unionised in the stomach
questions.exp: Aspirin (acidic) is unionised in the stomach because an acidic drug is unionised in an acidic medium - the same principle used for its absorption. (Book p5)

questions.q: Maximum absorption of unionised drug - whether acidic or basic - occurs in the:
opts: Small intestine (duodenum) because of its large surface area
Stomach because of its acidic pH
questions.exp: Although both acidic and basic drugs can be unionised in their corresponding media, maximum absorption takes place in the small intestine (duodenum) because of its large surface area. (Book p5)

questions.q: The dominant reason maximum unionised drug absorption occurs in the duodenum rather than the stomach is:
opts: There is a much larger surface area
The stomach contains more P-gp pumps
The stomach has a higher pH
Bile salts inactivate drug in the stomach
questions.exp: The book attributes maximum absorption of unionised drug in the small intestine/duodenum to its large surface area. (Book p5)

questions.q: Resection of the small intestine (short bowel syndrome) results in:
opts: Decreased absorption of the drug, managed by increasing the dose or changing the route
Increased absorption of the drug, requiring dose reduction
questions.exp: Short bowel syndrome reduces drug absorption; management is to increase the dosage of the drug or change the route of administration. (Book p5)

questions.q: For ionization to promote excretion of a drug, the pH of the drug and the pH of the medium must be:
questions.exp: Excretion depends on the pH of the drug and pH of the medium being different, which ionises the drug and prevents reabsorption. (Book p5)

questions.q: Acidic drug toxicity is treated by making the urine:
opts: Basic, using bicarbonate as a urine alkalinizer
questions.exp: Alkalinizing the urine with bicarbonate ionises acidic drugs and traps them for excretion - the standard treatment of acidic drug toxicity. (Book p5)

questions.q: Which drugs are listed as examples of acidic drug toxicity in which urine alkalinization is used?
questions.exp: Aspirin, phenobarbital and methotrexate are the acidic drugs whose toxicity is managed by alkalinizing urine with bicarbonate. (Book p5)

questions.q: Basic drug toxicity, as with amphetamine, is managed by:
opts: Making the urine acidic with ammonium chloride
Making the urine basic with bicarbonate
questions.exp: For basic drug toxicity the urine is made acidic with ammonium chloride (a urine acidifier), which ionises and traps the basic drug. (Book p5)

questions.q: Ammonium chloride is used as a:
questions.exp: Ammonium chloride is the urine acidifier used for basic drug toxicity such as amphetamine. (Book p5)

questions.q: Which of the following are also given as examples of urine acidifiers?
questions.exp: A note states that other examples of urine acidifiers are vitamin C and cranberry juice. (Book p5)

questions.q: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic drug is:
questions.exp: For an acidic drug the equation is log [unionized]/[ionized] = pKa - pH of the medium. (Book p6)

questions.q: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic drug is:
questions.exp: For a basic drug the ratio is inverted - log [ionized]/[unionized] = pKa - pH. (Book p6)

questions.q: An acidic drug with pKa = 4 is placed in the stomach at pH = 2. The unionized:ionized ratio will be:
For an acidic drug with pKa = 4 in the stomach (pH 2), the percentage of drug in the unionized form is:
questions.exp: Unionized:ionized = 100:1 gives 99% unionized and only 1% ionized - which is why such drugs are absorbed from the stomach. (Book p6)

questions.q: pKa is defined as the pH of the medium at which:
opts: 50% of the drug is ionized and 50% is unionized
questions.exp: pKa is the pH of the medium at which 50% of the drug is ionized and 50% is unionized. (Book p6)

questions.q: Immediate release (IR) oral formulations are characterised by:
opts: A prolonged plateau of plasma concentration
questions.exp: The IR graph shows repeated peaks with each dose; the mechanism is frequent dosing, which decreases compliance - the example given is indomethacin TID. (Book p6)

questions.q: Which formulation is given as an example of immediate release dosing three times a day?
questions.exp: Indomethacin TID is the example of an IR formulation requiring frequent dosing. (Book p6)

questions.q: Compared with IR preparations, sustained release (SR) preparations show:
opts: A shorter peak and an increased duration of action
A taller peak and a shorter duration of action
questions.exp: The SR graph is labelled 'shorter peak' with increased duration of action, which is why compliance improves. (Book p6)

questions.q: Extended release (ER) oral formulations are sub-classified into:
questions.exp: The flowchart shows tablet/capsule branching into IR, and 'ER: extended release' branching into SR (sustained release) and CR (controlled release). (Book p6)

questions.q: Controlled release (CR) preparations are also known as:
questions.exp: The book writes 'CR: controlled release AKA zero order CR' - a constant amount of drug is released per unit time, giving a flat plateau. (Book p6)

questions.q: The mechanism underlying controlled release formulations is:
opts: Enteric coating sensitive to gastric acid
questions.exp: CR tablets use polymer coating of pores so that drug is released slowly and steadily; the example is CR zolpidem. (Book p6)

questions.q: Which formulation is given as the example of a controlled release preparation?
questions.exp: CR zolpidem is the stated example of a controlled release preparation. (Book p6)

questions.q: SR indomethacin is described as having:
opts: Better compliance with polymer coating present
Zero order release with pore coating
questions.exp: For SR the book lists better compliance, polymer coating present, and the example SR indomethacin. (Book p6)

questions.q: On a plasma concentration-time graph, a preparation showing two successive peaks is:
questions.exp: The IR graph shows one peak per dose, so two doses produce two peaks; SR shows a flatter shorter peak and CR a plateau from a single dose. (Book p6)

questions.q: The plasma concentration-time curve of a controlled release preparation is distinctive because it:
opts: Rises and then stays flat (zero order plateau)
questions.exp: The CR graph rises and flattens into a plateau, reflecting zero order release; SR instead shows a shorter peak with prolonged duration. (Book p6)

questions.q: Delayed release preparations are designed to:
opts: Release the drug in the small intestine instead of the stomach
Release the drug immediately in the stomach
Release the drug only in the colon
questions.exp: Delayed release means release of the drug in the small intestine instead of in the stomach - the example given is sulfasalazine. (Book p7)

questions.q: Sulfasalazine is given as an example of a delayed release drug used for:
questions.exp: Sulfasalazine is the delayed release drug released in the small intestine, used for ulcerative colitis. (Book p7)

questions.q: Enteric coated preparations, such as proton pump inhibitors, are used to:
opts: Protect the drug from gastric HCl
Protect the stomach from the drug's irritant effect only
questions.exp: The book's example of enteric coating is a PPI, which is protected from gastric HCl so that it is released in the intestine. (Book p7)

questions.q: Bioavailability (f) is defined as the:
opts: Fraction of drug that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged
Total amount of drug absorbed from the gut
Rate at which the drug is absorbed
Fraction of drug excreted unchanged in urine
questions.exp: Bioavailability = the fraction of drug that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. (Book p7)

questions.q: In the flowchart of factors determining f, the fraction of absorbed drug that is lost on its first passage through the liver is called:
questions.exp: The flowchart shows that of 100% drug given, after intestinal absorption (with excretion of a fraction) the liver leaves a fraction reaching systemic circulation while a fraction undergoes first pass metabolism. (Book p7)

questions.q: Bioavailability (f) is increased when:
opts: The drug bypasses the liver and absorption is increased
The drug undergoes extensive first pass metabolism
A fraction of the drug is excreted in the gut
The drug is heavily protein bound
questions.exp: The book states f increases if the drug bypasses the liver and if absorption occurs to a greater extent. (Book p7)

questions.q: Bioavailability from a concentration-time curve is calculated as:
questions.exp: The boxed formula is Bioavailability = AUC oral / AUC IV x 100. (Book p7)

questions.q: Which route has 100% bioavailability?
questions.exp: IV is the only route with 100% bioavailability because the entire dose enters the systemic circulation directly. (Book p7)

questions.q: The area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) of a drug reflects:
opts: The rate of drug elimination only
questions.exp: The book relates AUC to the extent of drug absorption, while Tmax reflects the rate of absorption. (Book p7)

questions.q: In the plasma concentration-time curve comparing routes, the hatched larger area under the curve belongs to the:
questions.exp: The graph shows AUC IV (hatched, larger) versus AUC oral (smaller); oral bioavailability is the ratio of the two. (Book p7)

questions.q: As per the table, the bioavailability of the intravenous route is:
questions.exp: The route-bioavailability table gives IV = 1, IM/SC = 0.75-1.0 and oral = 0.05-1.0. (Book p8)

questions.q: The bioavailability of intramuscular/subcutaneous administration is:
questions.exp: IM/SC bioavailability is 0.75-1.0, higher than oral (0.05-1.0) because these routes avoid first pass metabolism. (Book p8)

questions.q: The oral route shows a bioavailability of:
questions.exp: Oral bioavailability ranges widely, 0.05-1.0, because of variable absorption and first pass metabolism. (Book p8)

questions.q: Which statement about bioavailability (f) is correct?
opts: f does not indicate the rate of drug absorption
f is the same as the rate of absorption
f equals Tmax of the drug
f is maximal for the oral route
questions.exp: The book notes that f does not indicate the rate of drug absorption - f is a measure of extent only. (Book p8)

questions.q: Cmax is defined as the:
opts: Maximum plasma concentration achieved by a drug
Time at which peak concentration occurs
questions.exp: Cmax is the maximum plasma concentration achieved by the drug, read off the peak of the concentration-time curve. (Book p8)

questions.q: Tmax is a marker of the:
questions.exp: Tmax - the time to reach peak plasma concentration - is the marker of the rate of drug absorption; AUC indicates extent. (Book p8)

questions.q: Which parameter pair tells you the RATE and the EXTENT of absorption respectively?
questions.exp: Tmax is the marker of rate of absorption and AUC indicates the extent of absorption - the basis of bioequivalence assessment. (Book p8)

questions.q: Two pharmaceutically equivalent compounds are said to be bioequivalent when they have similar:
questions.exp: Bioequivalence means two pharmaceutically equivalent compounds with similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption. (Book p8)

questions.q: A branded drug is one which is:
opts: A legal copy made after patent expiry
questions.exp: The branded drug is the invented, patented molecule, protected for 20 years. (Book p8)

questions.q: A generic drug is:
opts: A legal copy of a new drug, made after the patent expires
A drug invented and patented for 20 years
A drug available only as an injectable
A drug with a different active moiety
questions.exp: The generic drug is a legal copy of a new drug prepared after the patent expires, and its benefit is that it is cheaper. (Book p8)

questions.q: Generic drugs are approved through:
questions.exp: The book states that for generic drug approval an ANDA - Abbreviated New Drug Application - is filed. (Book p8)

questions.q: For a generic drug to be approved, it must be bioequivalent to the branded drug within:
questions.exp: The criterion for approval is that the generic drug is bioequivalent to the branded drug to within +/- 20%. (Book p8)

units.title: The Criteria Table: LUNA vs WIPE
units.guide: A single table decides whether a drug is absorbed or excreted. Absorption demands lipid solubility, the unionised form, a pH of medium equal to that of the drug and non-polar character - the mnemonic LUNA; excretion demands water solubility, the ionised form, unequal pH and polar character - WIPE.

units.title: Unionization: Stomach vs Small Intestine
units.guide: An acidic drug is unionised in the acidic stomach and a basic drug in the basic small intestine, so aspirin is unionised in gastric acid. Despite this, maximum absorption of any unionised drug occurs in the duodenum because of its enormous surface area - and when the small intestine is resected, as in short bowel syndrome, absorption falls and the dose must be raised or the route changed.

units.title: Ionization for Excretion: Urine pH Manipulation
units.guide: When the pH of the drug differs from that of the medium the drug is ionised and excreted. Acidic drug toxicity - aspirin, phenobarbital, methotrexate - is treated by alkalinizing urine with bicarbonate, while basic drug toxicity - amphetamine - is treated by acidifying urine with ammonium chloride; vitamin C and cranberry juice are other urine acidifiers.

units.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch: Quantifying Ionization
units.guide: For an acidic drug log [unionized]/[ionized] = pKa - pH, and for a basic drug log [ionized]/[unionized] = pKa - pH. An acidic drug of pKa 4 in gastric pH 2 gives a ratio of 100, i.e. 99% unionised and 1% ionised. pKa itself is the pH at which half the drug is ionised and half unionised.

units.title: IR, SR and CR Oral Formulations
units.guide: Tablets and capsules come as immediate release, which needs frequent dosing (indomethacin TID), or extended release, which splits into sustained release and controlled release. SR gives a shorter peak with longer duration of action, better compliance and a polymer coat (SR indomethacin); CR is zero order release from polymer-coated pores (CR zolpidem), drawn as a flat plateau on the concentration-time curve.

units.title: Drugs Bypassing the Stomach
units.guide: Delayed release formulations liberate the drug in the small intestine rather than the stomach - sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis - while enteric coating is used to protect acid-labile drugs such as proton pump inhibitors from gastric HCl.

units.title: Bioavailability: Definition and Formula
units.sec: Rate and Extent of Absorption · p7
units.guide: Bioavailability (f) is the fraction of drug reaching the systemic circulation unchanged. Of 100% drug absorbed, a fraction is excreted and a fraction is lost to first pass metabolism in the liver; f rises if the drug bypasses the liver or absorption increases. It is calculated as AUC oral/AUC IV x 100, reflects the extent of absorption, and is 100% only for the intravenous route.

units.title: f by Route, Cmax and Tmax
units.guide: The route table gives IV bioavailability 1, IM/SC 0.75-1.0 and oral 0.05-1.0. Crucially f tells only the extent, not the rate of absorption; the rate is judged from Tmax and the height of the curve by Cmax, the maximum plasma concentration achieved.

units.title: Branded, Generic and Bioequivalence
units.guide: Bioequivalence means two pharmaceutically equivalent products share a similar rate (Tmax) and extent (AUC) of absorption. A branded drug is the invented molecule patented for 20 years; a generic is a legal, cheaper copy made after patent expiry and approved through an ANDA, provided it is bioequivalent to the branded drug within +/- 20%.
